goals: Explain what Fa-hien's account tells us about society and administration
Explain the importance of the Allahabad Pillar Inscription and why it is read with care

Describe central, provincial and local administration under the Guptas

slides.heading: The Age of the Guptas: sources, kings and administration
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how we know about the Guptas, who ruled, and how they governed.

slides.narration: In this part we learn how historians know about the Gupta age. We meet the Gupta rulers in order, and then see how the king, his officers, provinces, districts, villages and towns shared the work of government.

slides.heading: Two main sources at a glance

rows: Travel account of a Chinese Buddhist monk, about 399 to 412 CE
Society and government in the time of Chandragupta II, seen by a visitor
Sanskrit eulogy by Harisena on an Ashokan pillar
The campaigns of Samudragupta and the rulers who submitted

visual.alt: Table of two sources: the account of Fa-hien, a Chinese monk who visited about 399 to 412 CE, and the Allahabad Pillar Inscription, a Sanskrit eulogy by Harisena about Samudragupta

slides.narration: Two sources are named in the syllabus. The first is the account of Fa-hien, a Chinese Buddhist monk who visited India. The second is the Allahabad Pillar Inscription, a Sanskrit eulogy composed by Harisena about Samudragupta. Each tells us something different, and each needs care.

slides.heading: Fa-hien, the Chinese pilgrim
bullets: A **Chinese Buddhist monk-pilgrim**.
Travelled in India about **399 to 412 CE**, in the reign of **Chandragupta II**.
Came to **collect Buddhist texts**.
He **does not name the king**; the link comes from the dates.

rows: About 399 to 412 CE, in the reign of Chandragupta II
He does not name the king; he is an outsider

visual.alt: Table about Fa-hien: a Chinese Buddhist monk-pilgrim who travelled about 399 to 412 CE in the reign of Chandragupta II to collect Buddhist texts, who does not name the king

slides.narration: Fa-hien was a Chinese Buddhist monk who travelled in India from about three hundred ninety nine to four hundred twelve of the common era. This was in the reign of Chandragupta the Second. He came to collect Buddhist texts. As commonly taught, he does not name the king, so historians link his visit with the king from the dates.

slides.heading: What the account describes
slides.body_md: Always paraphrase; never copy the pilgrim's words.

headers: What the account is commonly taught to describe
rows: Mild punishments, mostly fines; freedom of movement
Buddhist monasteries; charitable houses and free hospitals at Pataliputra
Religious support and care for the sick
Chandalas lived apart and were treated as outcastes

visual.alt: Table of what the account of Fa-hien is commonly taught to describe: a peaceful and prosperous land, mild punishments and freedom of movement, monasteries and hospitals, and Chandalas living apart as outcastes

slides.narration: As commonly taught, the account describes a peaceful and prosperous land. Punishments were mild, mostly fines, and people could travel freely. There were Buddhist monasteries, and charitable houses and free hospitals at Pataliputra. The account also notes that Chandalas lived apart and were treated as outcastes. So prosperity and exclusion appear together.

slides.heading: The Allahabad Pillar Inscription
bullets: Composed in **Sanskrit** by **Harisena**, a court poet and official of **Samudragupta**.
Engraved on an **earlier Ashokan pillar** now at Allahabad (Prayagraj).
Records **campaigns in the north and south** and the **rulers who submitted**.
A **prashasti** (eulogy): it praises the king, so **read with care**.

rows: Harisena, a court poet and official of Samudragupta
Engraved on an earlier Ashokan pillar, now at Allahabad (Prayagraj)
Campaigns in the north and south; rulers who submitted
A prashasti praises the king, so read with care

visual.alt: Table about the Allahabad Pillar Inscription: composed in Sanskrit by Harisena, engraved on an earlier Ashokan pillar at Allahabad, recording the campaigns of Samudragupta and rulers who submitted, and a eulogy to be read with care

slides.narration: The Allahabad Pillar Inscription is also called the Prayag Prashasti. Harisena, a court poet and official of Samudragupta, composed it in Sanskrit. It was engraved on an earlier pillar of the age of Ashoka, now at Allahabad. It records the campaigns of Samudragupta and the rulers who submitted. Because it is a eulogy, it praises the king, so a historian reads it with care.

slides.narration: Here is a simple method. Read the question the historian is asking. Choose the source that can answer it. Say what kind of source it is, and add one caution. For roads and justice we use Fa-hien and note that he was an outsider. For the rulers said to be defeated we use the inscription and note that it is a eulogy. For the size of the territory we use coins together with inscriptions.

slides.narration: The major Gupta rulers were Chandragupta the First, Samudragupta, Chandragupta the Second, Kumaragupta the First and Skandagupta. The bars are drawn roughly to scale. Chandragupta the First ruled from about three hundred twenty of the common era, and Skandagupta until about four hundred sixty seven. Books differ a little, so always say about.

slides.heading: The early Guptas and Chandragupta I
bullets: **Sri Gupta** is the founder in **tradition**, followed by **Ghatotkacha**.
**Chandragupta I**, about **320 to 335 CE**.
The **Gupta era** begins about **319 to 320 CE**.
His marriage to the **Lichchhavi** princess **Kumaradevi** strengthened his position.

Ghatotkacha
Chandragupta I marries Kumaradevi, about 320 CE

visual.alt: Flow: Sri Gupta, founder in tradition, then Ghatotkacha, then Chandragupta I who married the Lichchhavi princess Kumaradevi and whose reign begins the Gupta era about 319 to 320 CE
visual.caption: The early Guptas.

slides.narration: In tradition, Sri Gupta founded the line, and Ghatotkacha followed him. Chandragupta the First ruled from about three hundred twenty to three hundred thirty five of the common era. The Gupta era begins about three hundred nineteen or twenty. His marriage to Kumaradevi, a Lichchhavi princess, linked his house with an important ruling clan and strengthened his position.

slides.heading: Samudragupta and Chandragupta II

rows: Military leader; campaigns in the Allahabad Pillar Inscription; patron of music (veena coins)
Defeated the Shakas of western India; nine gems linked by tradition

visual.alt: Table of two rulers: Samudragupta, about 335 to 375 CE, a military leader and patron of music, and Chandragupta II Vikramaditya, about 375 or 380 to 415 CE, who defeated the Shakas

slides.narration: Samudragupta ruled from about three hundred thirty five to three hundred seventy five. He was a military leader, and the inscription records his campaigns. He was also a patron of music, and some coins show him playing the veena. Chandragupta the Second, also called Vikramaditya, defeated the Shakas of western India. By tradition, the nine gems are linked with his court.

slides.heading: Kumaragupta I and Skandagupta

rows: Nalanda traditionally linked with his reign

visual.alt: Table of two later rulers: Kumaragupta I, about 415 to 455 CE, linked with Nalanda by tradition, and Skandagupta, about 455 to 467 CE, who resisted the Huna invasions

slides.narration: Kumaragupta the First ruled from about four hundred fifteen to four hundred fifty five, and Nalanda is traditionally linked with his reign. Skandagupta followed him, from about four hundred fifty five to four hundred sixty seven, and he resisted the Huna invasions. Remember the order of all five rulers.

visual.caption: Gupta administration (simplified).

slides.narration: This chart shows the administration in simple form. The king, with the title Maharajadhiraja, stood at the top and was assisted by ministers and high officers. Below him were provinces, districts and villages, each with its own head. Towns had councils in which guilds were represented.

slides.heading: The centre: king and officers
bullets: Grand titles such as **Maharajadhiraja**.
**Kumaramatya**: high officers.
**Sandhivigrahika**: minister of peace and war.
**Mahadandanayaka**: chief judicial or military officer.

rows: Grand titles such as Maharajadhiraja; assisted by ministers

visual.alt: Table of the central administration: the king with titles such as Maharajadhiraja, the kumaramatya as high officer, the sandhivigrahika as minister of peace and war, and the mahadandanayaka as chief judicial or military officer

slides.narration: At the centre the king took grand titles such as Maharajadhiraja, and ministers assisted him. The kumaramatyas were high officers. The sandhivigrahika was the minister of peace and war. The mahadandanayaka was a chief judicial or military officer. Titles and duties vary a little between books.

slides.heading: Provinces, districts and villages
bullets: **Province** (**bhukti**) under an **uparika**.
**District** (**vishaya**) under a **vishayapati**.
**Village** headed by a **gramika** with **elders**.

nodes.label: Province (bhukti) under an uparika
District (vishaya) under a vishayapati
Village under a gramika with elders

visual.alt: Flow: province called a bhukti under an uparika, district called a vishaya under a vishayapati, and village under a gramika with elders
visual.caption: Levels below the centre.

slides.narration: The empire was divided into provinces called bhuktis, each under an uparika. Provinces had districts called vishayas, each under a vishayapati. A village was headed by a gramika, who worked with the village elders. In this way orders and local decisions moved between the centre and the villages.

slides.heading: Towns, revenue and a comparison
bullets: Towns had **councils** with **guild representatives**.
Land revenue commonly **about one-sixth** of the produce.
More **decentralised** than the Mauryan system.

rows: Commonly about one-sixth of the produce
More decentralised: more left to local bodies

visual.alt: Table of town councils with guild representatives, land revenue about one-sixth of produce, and the comparison that Gupta administration was more decentralised than the Mauryan

slides.narration: Towns had councils with representatives of the guilds. Land revenue was commonly about one sixth of the produce. When we compare with the Mauryan empire, Gupta administration was more decentralised, because village elders and town councils did much of the local work.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: planning a 10-mark answer
slides.body_md: Question: (i) The king and officers. [3] (ii) Provinces, districts, villages. [3] (iii) Towns, revenue, comparison. [4]
bullets: (i) King with titles; ministers; two officers.
(ii) Bhukti and uparika; vishaya and vishayapati; gramika.
(iii) Town councils; one-sixth; more decentralised.
Aim for one point per mark.

rows: King with titles; ministers; two named officers
Bhukti and uparika; vishaya and vishayapati; gramika with elders
Town councils; revenue about one-sixth; comparison with the Mauryas

visual.alt: Table planning a ten-mark answer on administration: part (i) king and officers for 3 marks, part (ii) provinces, districts and villages for 3 marks, part (iii) town councils, revenue and comparison for 4 marks

slides.narration: To plan a ten mark answer in three parts, give three points to the first part, three to the second and four to the last. Part one covers the king and two named officers. sections.heading: 1. Sources: Fa-hien and the Allahabad Pillar Inscription
sections.body_md:
- **Fa-hien (Faxian):** a Chinese Buddhist monk-pilgrim who travelled in India about **399 to 412 CE**, in the reign of **Chandragupta II**, to collect Buddhist texts. As commonly taught, his account describes a peaceful and prosperous land, mild punishments (mostly fines), freedom of movement, Buddhist monasteries, and charitable houses and free hospitals at Pataliputra. He also notes that the **Chandalas** lived apart and were treated as outcastes. He does not name the king.
- **Allahabad Pillar Inscription (Prayag Prashasti):** composed in **Sanskrit** by **Harisena**, a court poet and official of **Samudragupta**; engraved on an **earlier Ashokan pillar** now at Allahabad (Prayagraj). It records Samudragupta's campaigns in the north and south and the rulers who submitted. It is a **prashasti** (eulogy), so it praises the king and is read with care.

A group that, in the account, lived apart from others.

sections.heading: 3. The Gupta kings in order
sections.body_md:
- **Sri Gupta** (founder in tradition) and **Ghatotkacha**.
- **Chandragupta I** (about 320 to 335 CE): marriage with the Lichchhavi princess **Kumaradevi** strengthened his position. The **Gupta era** begins about 319 to 320 CE.
- **Samudragupta** (about 335 to 375 CE): a military leader and a patron of music; coins show him playing the veena. (A modern historian, V. A. Smith, called him the "Napoleon of India", a comparison that is debated.)
- **Chandragupta II Vikramaditya** (about 375 or 380 to 415 CE): defeated the **Shakas** of western India; by tradition the **nine gems (navaratnas)** are linked with his court.
- **Kumaragupta I** (about 415 to 455 CE): Nalanda is traditionally linked with his reign.
- **Skandagupta** (about 455 to 467 CE): resisted the **Huna** invasions.
- Dates are approximate and books vary; say **about**.

sections.heading: 4. Gupta administration
sections.body_md:
- **Centre:** the king took grand titles such as **Maharajadhiraja** and was assisted by ministers. Officers as commonly taught: **kumaramatya** (high officers), **sandhivigrahika** (minister of peace and war), **mahadandanayaka** (chief judicial or military officer).
- **Provinces (bhukti)** were under an **uparika**; **districts (vishaya)** under a **vishayapati**; a **village** was headed by a **gramika** with elders.
- **Towns** had councils with **guild representatives**. Land revenue was commonly about **one-sixth** of the produce.
- Gupta administration was **more decentralised** than the Mauryan.

sections.heading: 5. Education and science: Nalanda, Aryabhatta and Sushruta
sections.body_md:
- **Nalanda:** a great Buddhist **mahavihara** (monastery-university) in present-day **Bihar**, founded about the 5th century CE. It drew students from across Asia, and Xuanzang studied there in the 7th century. It had a library and taught many subjects, not only Buddhism. It declined in the late 12th century, and its ruins became a **UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016**.
- **Aryabhatta (Aryabhata):** born **476 CE**; wrote the **Aryabhatiya** about **499 CE**. He stated that the earth rotates on its axis, explained eclipses by the shadows of the earth and the moon, gave a close value of **pi** (about 3.1416) and worked with the place-value system. India's first satellite (1975) was named after him.
- **Sushruta Samhita:** a classic text on **medicine and surgery**; it describes many surgical instruments and procedures, including repair of the nose (an early form of plastic surgery), and stresses training and cleanliness. Its **date is debated**: the text was compiled and revised over centuries, and the syllabus studies it with the Gupta age.

sections.heading: 6. Culture: Kalidasa, Deogarh and the golden age
sections.body_md:
- **Kalidasa:** the greatest Sanskrit poet and playwright, traditionally linked with Chandragupta II's court. Plays: **Abhijnanashakuntalam**, **Malavikagnimitram**, **Vikramorvashiyam**. Long poems: **Raghuvamsha**, **Kumarasambhava**. Also **Meghaduta** and **Ritusamhara**.
- **Dashavatara temple, Deogarh:** in Lalitpur district, Uttar Pradesh, about the 6th century CE; dedicated to Vishnu; one of the earliest stone temples of north India. It stands on a raised platform (**jagati**) with a square sanctum and a **shikhara** that survives only in part; it is often described as of the **panchayatana** type. Carved panels include **Anantashayana** (Vishnu resting on Sheshanaga), **Gajendra moksha** and **Nara-Narayana**.
- **Golden age:** the age is often called a golden age for literature, science and art, but historians qualify the label because the prosperity and culture were mostly of the elite and caste rules grew stricter.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Giving a date without the word about.
- Saying that Fa-hien named the king, or quoting him.
- Treating the Allahabad Pillar Inscription as the complete truth; it is a eulogy.
- Mixing up uparika (province) and vishayapati (district).
- Writing that Sushruta lived under one Gupta king.
- Listing the Aryabhatiya as a work of Kalidasa.
- Saying the age was golden for everyone.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: one correct option, name or term.
- 2 marks: two distinct points; 3 marks: three points.
- 10-mark questions in 3 + 3 + 4 parts: one clear point per mark; the last part usually needs a reason, a link or an evaluation.

questions.stem_md: A student in an imagined Class IX history club says, "Fa-hien tells us in his book that Chandragupta II was a great ruler." Which reply is the most accurate?

options.text_md: Fa-hien names Samudragupta in every chapter
Fa-hien does not name the king; historians link his visit of about 399 to 412 CE with Chandragupta II from the dates
Fa-hien was a Gupta minister who wrote the king's orders
Fa-hien wrote only about Nalanda and not about the land

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Fa-hien does not name the king; historians link his visit of about 399 to 412 CE with Chandragupta II from the dates. The account describes the land and its people but, as commonly taught, does not name the king; the link with Chandragupta II comes from the dates. He was a Chinese monk, not a minister, and he wrote about many places.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined discussion, a teacher notes that Fa-hien found the land peaceful and prosperous but also records that Chandalas lived apart and were treated as outcastes. What should a historian conclude?

options.text_md: There was no inequality of any kind in Gupta society
Chandalas governed the towns where they lived
The account cannot be used at all as a source
Conditions were not the same for everyone: the account shows prosperity and also social exclusion of some groups

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Conditions were not the same for everyone: the account shows prosperity and also social exclusion of some groups. A careful reading keeps both observations: a prosperous land and a society in which some groups were excluded. The account is a useful source, though not a perfect one; the other options contradict it.

questions.stem_md: An imagined student prepares a chart headed "What Fa-hien's account is commonly taught to say about the Gupta land". Which entry belongs on the chart?

options.text_md: Punishments were mostly mild, often fines, and travellers could move about freely
Every traveller needed a royal pass at each town
Buddhist monasteries had all been closed
The pilgrim was received by the king in a grand court procession

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Punishments were mostly mild, often fines, and travellers could move about freely. As commonly taught, the account describes mild punishments, mostly fines, and freedom of movement. It also mentions Buddhist monasteries, so closure is wrong, and it does not claim a royal pass or a procession.

questions.stem_md: A student in an imagined debate says, "Every claim in the Allahabad Pillar Inscription must be exactly true, because it was carved in stone." Which reply is the most accurate?

options.text_md: It is true in every line, because stone cannot be changed
It is false in every line, because a poet wrote it
It is a prashasti, a eulogy meant to praise the king, so it should be read with care and checked against other evidence such as coins
It says nothing about the ruler's campaigns

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It is a prashasti, a eulogy meant to praise the king, so it should be read with care and checked against other evidence such as coins. A prashasti is written to praise, so a historian reads it with care and compares it with other evidence. It is not true in every line or false in every line, and it does record the campaigns.

questions.stem_md: A researcher in an imagined library wants a list of the northern and southern rulers who, according to a court record, submitted to Samudragupta. Which source should she open first?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The Allahabad Pillar Inscription. The inscription records Samudragupta's campaigns and the rulers who submitted. Fa-hien wrote about a later visit and about the land, the Samhita is a medical text, and the ruins of Nalanda belong to a monastery-university.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The Prayag Prashasti was composed in Sanskrit by Harisena, a court poet and official of Samudragupta.
questions.solution_md: **True.** True. Harisena composed it in Sanskrit, and it was engraved on an earlier Ashokan pillar now at Allahabad (Prayagraj).

questions.stem_md: Fa-hien, who visited India about 399 to 412 CE, came from the country of ___.
questions.solution_md: He came from China: Fa-hien was a Chinese Buddhist monk-pilgrim.

questions.stem_md: Match each term connected with the sources of Gupta history with what it is.

match_right.text_md: Court poet who composed the Prayag Prashasti

Chinese monk-pilgrim who visited India about 399 to 412 CE

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Fa-hien was the Chinese pilgrim, Harisena the poet, a prashasti is a eulogy, and the Allahabad pillar is an Ashokan pillar that was later engraved with the inscription.

questions.stem_md: State two things that the account of Fa-hien tells us about life in the Gupta land.
questions.solution_md: Any two: peace and mild punishments; monasteries and hospitals; freedom of travel.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. He describes a **peaceful and prosperous** land where **punishments were mild**, mostly fines.
2. He notes **Buddhist monasteries** and **charitable houses and free hospitals** at Pataliputra, and that people could **travel freely**.

questions.stem_md: Why is the Allahabad Pillar Inscription important as a source for Samudragupta?
questions.solution_md: Harisena; campaigns and rulers who submitted.

answer.model_answer_md: It was composed by **Harisena**, a court poet and official, and it records Samudragupta's **campaigns in the north and the south** and the **rulers who submitted**. It is therefore a main source for his reign.

questions.solution_md: Two sources with their authors and two cautions.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Fa-hien's account**: written by a Chinese monk who visited about 399 to 412 CE.
2. **Allahabad Pillar Inscription**: composed by Harisena in praise of Samudragupta.
3. **Care**: Fa-hien was an outsider who does not name the king, and the inscription is a **eulogy**, so both must be checked against other evidence.

questions.stem_md: A family tree drawn by students of an imagined school shows that one early Gupta ruler married the Lichchhavi princess Kumaradevi, which strengthened his position. Whose name belongs at the top of the tree?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Chandragupta I. Chandragupta I is the ruler associated with the marriage to Kumaradevi. Ghatotkacha came before him in tradition, and Kumaragupta I and Skandagupta ruled later.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined coin gallery, a gold coin shows a king seated and playing the veena. Which ruler, a military leader and also a patron of music, do such coins suggest?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Samudragupta. Coins showing the king with a veena are linked with Samudragupta, who was a military leader and a patron of music. Skandagupta is remembered for resisting the Hunas, and the others are known for other reasons.

questions.stem_md: A teacher in an imagined classroom says: "This ruler took the title Vikramaditya after defeating the Shakas of western India." Which ruler is meant?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Chandragupta II. Chandragupta II, also called Vikramaditya, is the ruler who defeated the Shakas of western India. The others are known for the marriage with Kumaradevi, for the southern and northern campaigns, and for a long peaceful reign.

questions.stem_md: A guide at an imagined fort exhibition says that the last great ruler of the early Gupta line spent much of his reign resisting invaders called the Hunas. Whom does she mean?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Skandagupta. Skandagupta (about 455 to 467 CE) is the ruler who resisted the Huna invasions. Samudragupta and Chandragupta II ruled earlier, and Sri Gupta is regarded in tradition as the founder of the line.

questions.stem_md: An imagined museum label gives the reigns of Chandragupta II as about 375 to 415 CE and of Kumaragupta I as about 415 to 455 CE. About how many years did the two reigns cover together?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** About 80 years. Each reign is about 40 years, and 40 plus 40 gives about 80. The others come from counting one reign only, adding a third reign, or dropping a digit.

questions.solution_md: **True.** True. Chandragupta II (about 375 or 380 to 415 CE) is commonly called Vikramaditya.

questions.stem_md: State two facts about Samudragupta.
questions.solution_md: Military campaigns; patron of music.

answer.model_answer_md:

questions.stem_md: State two points about Chandragupta II Vikramaditya.
questions.solution_md: Defeated the Shakas; nine gems by tradition.

answer.model_answer_md:

questions.stem_md: Give one important fact each about Chandragupta I, Kumaragupta I and Skandagupta.
questions.solution_md: One fact for each of the three rulers.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Chandragupta I** (about 320 to 335 CE): his marriage to the Lichchhavi princess **Kumaradevi** strengthened his position; the Gupta era begins about 319 to 320 CE.
2. **Kumaragupta I** (about 415 to 455 CE): by tradition, the great centre of learning at **Nalanda** belongs to his reign.

questions.stem_md: An imagined student draws a timeline that puts Skandagupta before Samudragupta and gives the reign of Chandragupta I as about 455 to 467 CE. Correct the two mistakes.
questions.solution_md: Correct order and dates.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Skandagupta** ruled last, about **455 to 467 CE**, after Samudragupta, Chandragupta II and Kumaragupta I.
2. **Samudragupta** ruled about **335 to 375 CE**, soon after Chandragupta I.
3. **Chandragupta I** ruled about **320 to 335 CE**, the earliest of the five.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined office chart at a school exhibition, a card reads: "I advise the king on whether to make peace or go to war." Which Gupta official does the card represent?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The sandhivigrahika. The sandhivigrahika is commonly taught as the minister of peace and war. The gramika headed a village, the vishayapati a district and the uparika a province.

questions.stem_md: On an imagined heritage trail, a board says: "A bhukti was one of the large divisions of the empire." Who headed a bhukti?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** An uparika. A bhukti (province) was under an uparika. A vishayapati headed a vishaya (district), a gramika a village, and a mahadandanayaka was a high judicial or military officer at the centre.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined Gupta-age village called Devpur, a dispute over a boundary is first heard by the headman together with the elders. What was the headman called?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Gramika. A village was headed by a gramika, assisted by village elders. The uparika, kumaramatya and vishayapati held higher offices.

questions.stem_md: An imagined farmer, Madan, harvests 90 quintals of grain. If land revenue was commonly about one-sixth of the produce, how much would be due?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** About 15 quintals. One-sixth of 90 is 15. Thirty would be one-third, 9 is one-tenth, and 60 is two-thirds.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined Gupta-age town of Chandanpur, the council that helps run the town includes a representative of the cloth merchants' guild and one of the potters' guild. What does this show?

options.text_md: The king alone decided every matter in the town
Towns had councils in which guilds were represented, so some local matters were handled locally
Towns had no administration at all

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Towns had councils in which guilds were represented, so some local matters were handled locally. Town councils with guild representatives show a share of local self-management. The other options deny local bodies or guilds.

questions.stem_md: An imagined student compares the Mauryan and Gupta administrations and notes that village elders and town councils did much local work in Gupta times. Which conclusion is the best supported?

options.text_md: Gupta administration was more decentralised, leaving more to local bodies, than the Mauryan
Gupta administration was exactly the same as the Mauryan in every detail
The Gupta king had no officials
There were no villages in Gupta times

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Gupta administration was more decentralised, leaving more to local bodies, than the Mauryan. Local bodies sharing the work point to a more decentralised system than the Mauryan one. The other options ignore the evidence or exaggerate.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Gupta administration is described as more decentralised than the Mauryan.

**Reason (R):** Villages had a gramika with elders and towns had councils with guild representatives, who handled many local matters.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and the reason explains the assertion: the sharing of local work with these bodies is what makes the system more decentralised.

questions.stem_md: In Gupta administration, the head of a village was called the ___.
questions.solution_md: The village head was the gramika.

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(s), (b)–(q), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). A kumaramatya was a high officer, the sandhivigrahika dealt with peace and war, the uparika headed a province and the vishayapati a district.

answer.model_answer_md: The king took grand titles such as **Maharajadhiraja** and was assisted by **ministers**. Officers included the **kumaramatya** (high officer) and the **sandhivigrahika** (minister of peace and war).

questions.stem_md: How was the empire divided for administration under the Guptas? Name the heads of the divisions.
questions.solution_md: Bhukti and uparika; vishaya and vishayapati.

answer.model_answer_md: The empire was divided into **provinces (bhukti)** under an **uparika** and **districts (vishaya)** under a **vishayapati**. A village was headed by a **gramika** with elders.

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons why historians describe Gupta administration as more decentralised than the Mauryan.
questions.solution_md: Village elders; town councils and guilds.

answer.model_answer_md: **Village elders** with the **gramika** managed local matters. **Town councils** with **guild representatives** also shared the work, so less was decided only by the centre.

questions.stem_md: Describe the central, provincial and local administration of the Guptas, one point each.
questions.solution_md: Centre; provinces and districts; local bodies.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Centre**: the king, with titles such as Maharajadhiraja, was helped by **ministers** and officers like the kumaramatya.
2. **Provinces and districts**: **bhukti** under an **uparika**; **vishaya** under a **vishayapati**.
3. **Local**: a **gramika** with village elders, and **town councils** with guild representatives.

questions.stem_md: The imagined town of Chandanpur has a council with representatives of the guilds. Explain, in three points, how such a council helped the Gupta administration.
questions.solution_md: Local matters; guild knowledge; shared work.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It let **local matters** be handled in the town itself.
2. **Guild representatives** brought the knowledge of **trade and crafts** into decisions.
3. It **shared the work** with the king's officers, which is why the system is called **more decentralised**.

questions.stem_md: An imagined student from a distant land writes home: "The mahavihara I joined in Bihar has a large library, and we study many subjects, not only the teachings of the Buddha." Which institution is he describing?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Nalanda. Nalanda was a great Buddhist monastery-university in present-day Bihar with a library, and it taught many subjects. Deogarh is a temple, Prayagraj is a city with a pillar, and a council is not a place of learning.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined pilgrim's notebook exhibit, two cards show Chinese monks: one visited India about 399 to 412 CE and one studied at Nalanda in the 7th century. Which pair is matched correctly?

Fa-hien in the 5th century, Xuanzang in the 7th century

questions.stem_md: The imagined Tara Astronomy Club asks why the stars seem to circle the sky every night. Which Gupta-age astronomer stated that the earth rotates on its axis?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Aryabhatta. Aryabhatta (born 476 CE) stated that the earth rotates on its axis. Sushruta is linked with medicine and surgery, Harisena with a poem in praise of a king, and Fa-hien with a travel account.

questions.stem_md: During an imagined eclipse watch, a club member explains it as the shadow of the earth falling on the moon. Whose explanation, in the Gupta age, does this match?

options.text_md: Kalidasa, who explained eclipses in a play
Aryabhatta, who explained eclipses by the shadows of the earth and the moon
Harisena, who recorded eclipses in an inscription

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Aryabhatta, who explained eclipses by the shadows of the earth and the moon. Aryabhatta explained eclipses by shadows of the earth and moon. The others are linked with literature, medicine and an inscription, not with the explanation of eclipses.

questions.stem_md: A card in an imagined museum of medicine describes an early text that lists surgical instruments, stresses training and cleanliness, and describes repairing a damaged nose. Which text is it?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The Sushruta Samhita. The Sushruta Samhita describes instruments and surgical procedures, including repair of the nose. The Aryabhatiya is on astronomy and mathematics, the Prashasti is an inscription, and the Meghaduta is a poem.

questions.stem_md:

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Fa-hien** was a **Chinese Buddhist monk-pilgrim** who travelled in India about **399 to 412 CE**, in the reign of **Chandragupta II**, to collect **Buddhist texts**.

(ii) He describes a **peaceful and prosperous** land with **mild punishments**, mostly fines, **freedom of movement**, **Buddhist monasteries** and **charitable houses and free hospitals** at Pataliputra. He also notes that **Chandalas lived apart** and were treated as outcastes.

(iii) The inscription was composed in Sanskrit by **Harisena**, engraved on an earlier **Ashokan pillar** at Allahabad, and records Samudragupta's **campaigns** and the rulers who submitted. It is a **prashasti**, a **eulogy**, so it praises the king and must be **checked against other evidence**.

answer.model_answer_md:

(ii) Samudragupta was a **military leader** whose campaigns in the north and the south are recorded in the **Allahabad Pillar Inscription**. He was also a **patron of music**: coins show him playing the **veena**.

(iii) Chandragupta II **defeated the Shakas** of western India and took the title **Vikramaditya**; by **tradition** the **nine gems** are linked with his court, where **Kalidasa** is placed. **Skandagupta** is remembered for **resisting the Huna invasions**.

questions.stem_md:

questions.solution_md: King and officers; provinces, districts and villages; town councils, revenue and comparison.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The king took grand titles such as **Maharajadhiraja** and was assisted by **ministers** in running the empire. Officers included the **kumaramatya** (high officer), the **sandhivigrahika** (minister of peace and war) and the **mahadandanayaka** (chief judicial or military officer).

(ii) A **province (bhukti)** was under an **uparika**, who acted for the king, and a **district (vishaya)** under a **vishayapati**. A **village** was headed by a **gramika** who worked with the **village elders** on local matters.

(iii) **Towns** had **councils** with representatives of **guilds**, so trade and crafts had a voice. **Land revenue** was commonly about **one-sixth** of the produce. Compared with the Mauryan system, Gupta administration was **more decentralised**, because more work was left to local bodies such as these.

marking_scheme.step: (ii) Bhukti and uparika; vishaya and vishayapati

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Nalanda was in present-day **Bihar**. It was a great **Buddhist monastery-university (mahavihara)** founded about the **5th century CE**, and tradition links it with the reign of **Kumaragupta I**.

(ii) Its **library** and its teaching of **many subjects**, not only Buddhism, made it a true centre of learning. It attracted **students from across Asia**, and the Chinese pilgrim **Xuanzang** studied there in the **7th century**, which shows how far its fame travelled.

(iii) Nalanda **declined in the late 12th century**, and its buildings fell into ruin over time. Its **ruins** were recognised as a **UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016**, which shows their value today as a record of ancient education and a reminder of the learning that once flourished there.

marking_scheme.step: (i) Tradition links it with Kumaragupta I

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Aryabhatta**, born in **476 CE**, wrote the **Aryabhatiya** in about **499 CE**. He stated that the **earth rotates on its axis**, explained **eclipses** by the shadows of the earth and the moon, and gave a close value of **pi** (about 3.1416) with the **place-value system**.

(ii) The **Sushruta Samhita** is a classic text on **medicine and surgery**. It describes many **surgical instruments** and procedures, including **repair of the nose** (an early form of plastic surgery), and stresses **training and cleanliness**.

(iii) The text was **compiled and revised over centuries** and its **date is debated**, so it is studied with the Gupta age without claiming that Sushruta lived under one Gupta king. India's **first satellite, launched in 1975**, was named **Aryabhata** after him.

marking_scheme.step: (iii) Text compiled and revised, date debated

(ii) The temple, in **Lalitpur district, Uttar Pradesh**, is dedicated to **Vishnu** and dates from about the **6th century CE**. It stands on a raised **platform (jagati)** with a **square sanctum** and a **shikhara** that survives only in part.
